utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And, Mr. Groome, it was announced last week that you would like to make a submission in relation to the way in which the Prosecution intends to present the evidence of Ms. Tabeau. Now, we could do it immediately before she arrives, but another way of dealing with it would be to make that submission now so as to give an opportunity to the Defence to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Marcus was going to do this. I do have her notes, so I can do that now, or we can do it at the beginning of the second session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if these are her submissions, then perhaps it would be better to wait for the first -- until after the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask her to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then since there are no other preliminaries, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And the next witness to be called, Mr. Groome, is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is General Richard Dannatt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, I use the time to briefly deal with D330. On the 11th of July the Chamber admitted video Exhibit D330 with instructions to the Defence to upload a corrected English transcript. The Defence indicated through informal correspondence on the 3rd of October that it had uploaded the correct English translation of the video. However, the Prosecution responded the same day stating that a line was still missing from the transcript. To the Chamber's knowledge, there was no further reply from the Defence on the matter. The Chamber has reviewed the video and notes that the interpretation of what the accused says in portion of the video appears to correspond with what the Prosecution has stated is missing from the transcript. The Chamber considers that the transcript should reflect what is said in the video and, therefore, instructs the Defence to upload a further corrected transcript no later than the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dannatt, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Dannatt, if I address you as Mr. Dannatt and not by rank or title that is not to express in any way a lack of appreciation for titles or ranks, but it is the way in which the Chamber usually addresses witnesses who come to tell us the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Groome. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, can we begin by having you place your name on the record, your full name?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: My name is Francis Richard Dannatt, and I was a general in the British army until 2009 when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What offices do you presently hold?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Currently I'm constable of Her Majesty's Tower of London and I sit as a cross bench, that's an independent member of the House of Lords in the British parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Dannatt, paragraph 7 to 22 of your report, which we will have before us in a few moments, sets out in some detail your professional training and experience. In short, you describe your military training and experience during a career between 1971 and 2009, a career that culminated with your appointment as Chief of the General Staff, the professional head of British Armed Forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That is correct, except I joined the British army in 1969 and my first two years were as an officer cadet under training and I commissioned as an officer in 1971.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask you to slow down because the interpreters have a difficult task in following your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, in the fall of 2011, did I ask you whether you were willing to serve as an expert in this trial --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, you did. You asked me and I agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And part of -- well, what you were asked to do was to examine a set of documents and answer a series of questions based upon your study of those documents as well as based on your expertise as a military commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And I examined those documents and produced a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, could I ask that 65 ter number 28317 be brought to our screens. It is a document dated 23 April 2012 and entitled, "Statement of General Dannatt." It was officially filed with the Chamber on the 24th of April, 2012. And, Your Honours, I have a clean, hard copy of this document. Could I ask that the witness have this before him during his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may the hard copy be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, we can now see 65 ter 28317 before us. Is this your report?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to the last page of this document so that we can see the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this is indeed your report?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It is dated the 23rd of April, 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask for this document to be marked for identification. I will tender it formally at the conclusion of General Dannatt's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28317 receives number P2629, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask at this time that 65 ter 28317A be brought to our screens. Your Honours, General Dannatt prepared his report prior to the commencement of the trial, and, thus, the citations in the report refer to 65 ter numbers and ERN numbers. To assist the Chamber in working with the report, we have prepared a chart of the documents referred to in it with citations to the exhibit numbers of documents which have now been admitted. I would ask that this document be marked for identification and I will tender it formally as a demonstrative exhibit when I tender the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28317A receives number P2630, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, in paragraph 3 of your report, you set out your understanding of your task. In paragraph 4 you state -- and I if I could ask that we return to P2629, this is on the first page in both versions. In paragraph 4 you state: "On occasion, I have requested additional material to satisfy myself on certain points of detail." My question is: Do you consider that you had access to a sufficient body of documentary evidence regarding the Army of the Republika Srpska to make comprehensive and reliable conclusions about the command function of that army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do, and I asked for additional material and it was provided, and I felt I had sufficient on which to base my conclusions and opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we look at the analysis and opinions contained in your report, I want to spend some time discussing your qualifications. I will not ask you to repeat the details of the comprehensive biography you have provided in your report, but do want you to address some particular points which may be relevant for the Chamber in its consideration of whether to recognise you as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again ask that the speakers make a short pause between question and answer and answer and question and that they slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, have you been recognised by a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal as an expert in matters related to commanding -- command and control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in a trial in the case against General Krstic a number of years ago, and was recognised as an expert in that case at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you been recognised by the Judges of the International Court of Justice as an expert on military matters related to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have, and similar matters were put to me in that previous trial as I believe will be put to me in this trial today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- you are talking about a trial where the question dealt with the International Court of Justice. Now, did you refer to the International Court of Justice or did you refer to your previous testimony before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I misheard the question. As well as giving evidence in this court, in a previous case, I did take part in another case at the International Court of Justice as an expert. I apologise. I misheard the question, but thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, that can be found on page 3 of the report in e-court, you state the following: "I was the lead author of army doctrine publications volume 1, operations, which set out a revised war fighting doctrine for the British army appropriate for the post-Cold War security environment." My question at this point is whether you were assigned the task of writing this manual and other publications you refer to because of your expertise in topics related to military command and control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was given this task because at the time, I was the colonel responsible for the higher command and staff course at the British army staff college, and rather as the name implies, that course teaches selected senior officers the art of war at the operational and strategic level, and to be able to do that, one has to have extensive knowledge not only of the way the British army operates but comparative knowledge of the way that other armies operate. And at the time, 1992/1993, in the immediate post-Cold War years, it's almost obvious that much of our focus on other military systems would have had us focusing on the Soviet model, an alternative model, and I had to become very conversant with that in order to sensibly frame a British army doctrine against the possible doctrines of other armies that we might find ourselves opposing. As we know, the world moved in a different direction but it was important to understand both the way we operated and the way that potential adversaries might operate. And against that background, I wrote the British army war fighting doctrine for the post-Cold War period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For what period of time did this publication remain in effect for the British army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It remained in effect until approximately 2005, which is about the length of time that I would expect it to remain in effect. The world doesn't stand still, and therefore any organisation, any military organisation, needs to keep reviewing its doctrine and the way that it conducts its business against the way the world is looking at any given moment. And the world looked one way in the immediate post-Cold War years throughout the 1990s, but after 9/11, the world began to look somewhat differently, and the British army, therefore, felt it was time again to revise its doctrine and a new doctrine was produced in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- it is only now that the B/C/S translation has finished. Could you please keep in mind to adapt your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraphs 12 and 14 to 15 - and this can be found in e-court pages 3 to 4 of both versions - you describe your deployments to the former Yugoslavia, in particular to Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as Kosovo, work that included, in part, the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accord. During this work, did you ever have occasion to meet with Ratko Mladic himself?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, sir. I have never met General Mladic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 11, you state that you were asked by Major-General Sir Michael Rose, then commander of UNPROFOR, to draft what you describe as a campaign plan for Bosnia, a plan you delivered to General Rose in February 1994. My question to you is: Do you know why you were selected for this task?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I was selected for that task by General Rose immediately prior to becoming commander of UNPROFOR. General Rose had been the komandant of the army staff college and I was on his staff as the colonel running the higher command and staff course, and writing the war-fighting doctrine which I've just referred to. He got in touch with me and said, You teach campaign planning at the staff college. I believe the operation by UNPROFOR in Bosnia needs greater clarity. I want you to put a team together and write me a campaign plan for Bosnia. So, effectively, he was asking me to do, in practical terms with regard to Bosnia, what I was teaching and studying in theoretical terms at the staff college. It was, as you can imagine, an interesting challenge, and one which I and the team of experts that I put together rose to with enthusiasm, and I then took that plan to Sarajevo and gave it to General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did your work on drafting this plan require you to become familiar with the armies of the respective sides in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did. But as you can imagine, the conflict in Bosnia had been running for some time by that moment, in early 1994, and, therefore, at the staff college we had been studying what was going on in Bosnia and in the former Yugoslavia considerably. So although at that stage in January 1994, I had not served in Bosnia, I had a good background knowledge of what was going on, and many of the instructors at the staff college had already served in Bosnia. I therefore built on my background understanding by asking many questions, conducting many interviews, conducting a lot of research, with the team of military experts that I assembled at the staff college in order to be able to produce this campaign plan for General Rose. Self-evidently, that plan had to be well-founded, well-researched, and of practical use, otherwise it would have not served its purpose for General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to the report itself. In paragraph 23, which can be found on e-court pages 5 in both versions, you state that there are certain basic principles that apply to all conventional armies, and you set out the first principle in paragraph 24, where the first sentence reads: "The first principle is that a superior commander gives orders to subordinate commanders who obey these orders and implement them." My question to you is whether there are differences in the way this principle is applied in the case of different national armies?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that that principle is a fundamental principle common to all armies, to all military organisations. Commanders give orders to subordinate commanders who obey those orders and carry them out. That is the way a military organisation functions in any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You set out the second principle in paragraph 25, where you state: "The second principle is that subordinates must report upwards the results of their actions to inform their superior of progress or otherwise in order for the higher command to carry out its own decision-making process." Again, I ask you whether there are differences in the way this principle is applied among national armies?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The basic principle is common to all armies. The way that it is conducted differs from army to army, somewhat dependent upon the military doctrine that a particular army follows. I'm very happy to elaborate that now, now or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask you some more detailed questions about that in a few moments, but before I do, could we return to the first principle, superiors give orders to subordinates. Can I ask you to enumerate the different ways in which a commander can give an order to a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: A commander can give an order to a subordinate in a variety of ways. He can issue a written directive, which is a general statement of future intentions. He can issue an operational order, which is a detailed statement of what is to be done. He can give orders in person, speaking person to person. He can give orders on the radio. He can give such orders in an abbreviated fashion using modern technology such as e-mails and texts. The underlying principle is that the subordinate must understand what the superior wants him to do, and there are a variety of ways in which that intimation of what the superior requires can be conveyed. There is no right way or wrong way to give an order. There are a variety of means. The important thing is that the meaning is understood and that the action will then be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does the fact that an order was given orally and not put in writing diminish the subordinate's obligation to comply with that order?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Not at all. Provided the intention has been clearly conveyed, any form of conveying the intention is equally legitimate. An oral order is perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it possible for an order to be given neither in written form or orally but simply through the use of a gesture?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think I would stand by my earlier answer, that provided the intention of the superior is accurately conveyed to the subordinate, it doesn't matter the means by which that intention is conveyed. If -- well, I use, I suppose, the historic example of gladiators fighting in the coliseum in Rome. When the culminating point of the engagement is reached, people looked to the emperor for either a thumbs up or a thumbs down, and we all know the implication of that. So I think a gesture is a perfectly acceptable way of conveying an intention but not the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your report at paragraphs 27 and 28 - this can be found at e-court page 7 in the original and 6 in the translation - you set out two general paradigms or concepts of military command, Auftragstaktik, or manoeuvrist approach to operations, and Befehlstaktik, an approach that relies on a centralised command. Can I ask you in a few sentences to describe for the Chamber the essential difference between the manoeuvrist approach and the centralised command approach?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I will. And I will try to be brief. These are both German terms. Auftragstaktik is a military doctrine best used by professional armies when the standard of training is high and the military education content, particularly of officers, is high, and it's a form of command and control which is intended to optimise the initiative of junior commanders. Very briefly, a superior commander would state his general intention, he would delegate tasks to individuals, and then expect them to use their initiative within the wider framework of his general intention to achieve the mission and to achieve the objective. And in this way, it means that the well-trained brains of junior commanders can be harnessed to better effect and to carry out the operation well. The third element of that system is that even though the superior commander will have delegated tasks, he has an absolute obligation to supervise the execution of those tasks, and he will do it either closely or less closely depending on his confidence in the subordinate to whom he's given the task. This is how a professional army that's well-trained operates. It characterises western armies, such as the British army, United States army, and is in very general terms the way that NATO armies try to operate. The other system known as Befehlstaktik, another German word, is a doctrine that is more centralised. It's characteristic of an army that is large, probably made up of conscripts, and where the level of training is lower. Under that system, there is not the flexibility and delegation that you find in Auftragstaktik, following armies that I've just described, by which I mean that a superior commander will give detailed instructions to his subordinates who will carry out those instructions, and when they are complete, the subordinate would expect to be given further instructions. So the key point that I'm trying to make is that under the centralised Befehlstaktik doctrine, there is much less scope for the use of initiative by junior commanders than there is in the other system that I have described. And as a final comment referring back to one of my other answers, under both systems, it is imperative that subordinates report upwards the results of their activities. Under the centralised Befehlstaktik doctrine, this would be done regularly and without fail and in some detail. Under Auftragstaktik, it is considered acceptable to only report when you have something of importance to say, and without putting it too simply, no news is good news, and the superior commander assumes that all is going according to plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just give the interpreters a moment now and then I'll ask my next question. On this issue of reporting, under Befehlstaktik or centralised command approach, what would typically happen if a report did not arrive when it was expected?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: If a report didn't arrive at the prescribed time, one would expect an operations staff officer from the superior headquarters to most probably get on the radio, or these days send an e-mail to the subordinate headquarters and say, Where is your report? What is the situation? What is going on? Why are you not keeping us in the picture? It would be chased up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You really have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It goes too fast for the interpreters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would now like to turn your attention to the VRS itself and your conclusions about its command and control systems. What type of command system was used by the VRS? Which of these models?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The VRS has the characteristic hallmarks of a centrally controlled army, following what I have described as the Befehlstaktik doctrine, and if I could explain why I think that is so: History will show that the VRS was formed from the army of the former Yugoslavia, and although Yugoslavia was not -- well, Yugoslavia was a looser member of the Warsaw Pact, and under Soviet influence. Nevertheless, the military system that the Yugoslav National Army followed was one very much influenced by the Soviet model, and that was a model based on centralised control characterised by Befehlstaktik which I've talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of your work, did you come to a view regarding how the first principle of militaries, superiors giving orders to subordinates, how this functioned in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. All my investigations show me that the Army of Republika Srpska operated in the way that I would expect any army to do, and that directives, operation orders, and sometimes verbal orders, were passed to subordinates to carry out missions and tasks in the classic fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 32, that can be found at 9 in the original, 8 in the translation, you describe an event when you were commander of the 4th Armoured Brigade on mission in Bosnia to implement the Dayton Peace Accord, and your efforts to meet with General Talic. What did that interaction or event demonstrate to you about the command structure of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Without going into detail of the situation at the time, whereas I had had routine meetings and discussions with the commanders of the Muslim and Croat forces, I had not had the opportunity to meet commander of the Bosnian Serb forces. And under Dayton, we were required to move into Republika Srpska and operate within the territorial area of Republika Srpska. I was concerned that although agreement had been reached at the strategic level at Dayton, that maybe the soldiers on the ground would not understand that NATO troops would be coming into Republika Srpska and that fighting would occur. And I decided that the way to ensure this didn't happen was that I would go to Banja Luka and see General Talic and confirm for myself with him that he understood his obligations under Dayton to allow my troops to cross into Republika Srpska and operate to implement the Dayton agreement. I let it be known through liaison officers that I was coming, and duly travelled to Banja Luka, but I was not able to meet General Talic because he had not received authority from General Mladic to see me. And I passed the message that I wanted to pass through liaison officers from General Talic's staff. What this told me was that General Talic had no delegated authority to make a decision on his own account to see me but that he would only do so if General Mladic, as the army commander, gave that authority. And that reinforced to me as an example the centralised command and control nature of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the penultimate sentence of paragraph 30, you state: "The culture of regularly reporting upward never changed, and indeed regulations required the upward passage of information." Can I ask you what did you base this conclusion about the reporting function of the VRS on, if you could summarise the basis for that view?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: In a number of documents that I saw, it was stated very clearly that there were reporting obligations placed on subordinate headquarters to send reports at certain time each day to their superior headquarters so that the superior headquarters was well-informed. I also looked at several documents at various stages during the conflict which were examples of those reports being sent from a brigade headquarters to its superior headquarters, and from a corps headquarters to the Main Staff headquarters. And even when the fighting became difficult and the war reached a climax in 1995, that system of upwards reporting remained in place as I would expect it to have done, and indeed my investigation showed that this indeed was the case, and that the command and control mechanism stayed in place and functioned effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask -- at this point in time I have one question: You told us about your wish to meet General Talic and you told us that he didn't get the permission by General Mladic. How do you know that? From whom did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The liaison officer who I spoke with was apologetic, and he told me that General Talic -- it was nothing personal, but that he had not received authority to see me, and therefore would I please convey my message through the liaison officer. There was a colonel and a captain. I'm afraid -- Captain Popovic was the name of the captain, and I have a picture of the colonel in my mind but I can't now remember his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that P353 be brought to our screens and I'm interested in an entry that spans e-court pages 246 to 272 in the original and 244 to 270 in the translation. So if we could please go to 244 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while that's being brought to our screens, last evening did I ask you to take a look at an entry from General Mladic's notebook?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We are still trying to bring up the English translation. Do you recall an entry in which Mladic records information he receives at a meeting that he has with municipal leaders?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I saw that last night. I currently am not looking at the English translation. Ah, I think I am now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is page 244. Could I ask that we go to 246. I may have reversed the English and translation. It's 246 in the English and 244 in the B/C/S, and the B/C/S is the transcription, not the original image. There we go for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the entry that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this notebook entry is in evidence and the Chamber will be able to study it. Can I ask you to summarise how this meeting, this meeting with local government officials, fits into the reporting requirement or the gathering of information by a commander in order to make command decisions?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: My answer to the question really has to be placed in the context of the kind of conflict which characterises the war in Bosnia, 1992 to 1995. Whereas in straightforward military operations, when one army is fighting another, in which case you would gather intelligence about the enemy, frame your plans and conduct operations, in this set of circumstances, it was very much as we describe as war amongst the people, the civilian population, the local communities, very much part and parcel of the background and the circumstances of the war. So it's absolutely inevitable and quite proper that military commanders at all levels have regular dialogue and regular meetings with civilian authorities, whether it's town mayors, local government ministers, local community leaders, and it's important that those civilian leaders understand what the military is doing and the military listens to what the civilian community wants to tell them. So civil-military relations are a very common characteristic of this kind of conflict, which is not pure war fighting in a simple force-on-force nature but it's within what one might call the messy and complex circumstances of what I've described as war amongst the people where the civilian population is absolutely critical as part of the background to what the militaries are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn your attention a different topic. General, you prepared your expert report before this trial began and your analysis was based on documentary evidence and some video materials. Prior to giving evidence today, did I provide you with the testimony of General Manojlo Milovanovic, General Mladic's Chief of Staff, and did I ask you to review that testimony?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you did. And I have read that and reviewed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you review it in its entirety, both the direct exam, the cross exam and the questions posed by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I have now done that. Initially, you provided me with some of it and more recently you provided me the whole transcript, which I have read, and it took quite some time to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you to provide us with any observations you may have, can I ask you to spend a few moments describing for the Chamber the role of a Chief of Staff to a commander?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff in any formation is in a unique position, in that not only is he, as the name implies, the Chief of Staff, the head of the staff, the leader of the headquarters, but he also acts as the deputy commander. Now, this isn't the case in every army. In the British army, the Chief of Staff will act as the deputy commander if the commander is away or incapacitated for any reason and he will hold command until a replacement commander is nominated. In the case of the Yugoslav National Army and therefore the Army of Republika Srpska, the Chief of Staff is the deputy commander and has singular authority to act in the command function if the commander is away. And therefore, when the commander is not present, the Chief of Staff in his capacity as deputy commander holds equal authority to the commander himself. So Chief of Staff is a very important position for those two reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Having read General Milovanovic's testimony, does it further inform your opinion regarding the Army of Republika Srpska? In other words, does it confirm your conclusions or cause you to amend them?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: From a professional military point of view, I was fascinated to read the entirety of General Milovanovic's testimony and cross-examination because it told me a lot about the origins of the Army of Republika Srpska, much of which I knew from my own research, but it was fascinating to me to read his description of what happened because it tallied with my understanding from my own research as to what happened. And from it, I could see that the Army of Republika Srpska undoubtedly had its origins in the former military district of the Yugoslav National Army, that the doctrine and regulations of the VRS were taken pretty much in entirety from the doctrine and regulations of the Yugoslav National Army which was a professional army of considerable competence, and that there was a functioning system of command and control that I recognised. And although it was a challenge in May, June, early part of 1992, to get the Army of Republika Srpska functioning quickly, given that a civil war was breaking out, this was achieved remarkably quickly because the doctrine and the regulations and many of the personnel were transferred en bloc from one army to the other. Moreover, it was very interesting to sense - I think that's the right word - from General Milovanovic's testimony, the significant presence of General Mladic as the commander of the Main Staff. It's quite clear that General Mladic was and is what I would describe as a big person, had a big personality, and that nothing that was done was not done without his authority. And on those occasions when General Mladic for one reason or another was away, away from the headquarters or out of the country, and General Milovanovic in his capacity as deputy commander took decisions, he was always very quick to ensure that General Mladic was informed of those decisions and his agreement was sought or if his agreement was not forthcoming then amendments were made to the decisions that had been taken. And this, to me, speaks volumes of the personality and character and style of command of General Mladic, and it came out very clearly to me in General Milovanovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that we are at the time for the break. Before I ask the next question, would we break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break now. Mr. Dannatt, we will take a break for you at least a little bit longer than usual. We usually have breaks of 20 minutes but since we have to hear some submissions immediately after the break, it may be a little bit over half an hour that you're excused. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, may I remind you, Mr. Mladic, that when you consult with counsel that you should speak at low volume, which is best achieved if you take out your ear-phones. We take a break and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, welcome in court, the Prosecution had announced that it would like to make submissions on the presentation of the evidence in relation to Ms. Tabeau. You have an opportunity to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Good morning. With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to distribute copies of the exhibit list for Dr. Tabeau. I've given the Registrar a few copies for the Chamber. I think it would facilitate an understanding of my submission. You have it, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have received it, yes, I [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sorry. Thank you, Your Honour. utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Would you like me to do that in court or via correspondence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Correspondence I think would be okay --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as long as it's copied to the Chamber staff and the Defence, then it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus, for these submissions. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic, for having given already a brief response. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Marcus, you are excused. Mr. Groome, as far as time is concerned, are we on track? I think you asked for one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm on track, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which, in fact, will mean that you do not need the whole of the session we are -- we will be in from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, Mr. Groome will now continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, I want to draw your attention and seek your comment on a few specifics elements of General Milovanovic's testimony. At transcript 16932, he said: "The command function has to be and it was in our military centralised. It was continuous and every activity had to finish with an analysis exercise. In the meantime, between the analysis and the previously issued order, there is the supervision or control of how the order is implemented." Can I ask you to comment on that testimony and help us understand it within the conceptual framework that you set out earlier today?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. This is a clear description of how a military organisation, an army, based on a centralised command philosophy would function, and that's what General Milovanovic is saying is that a task is decided, orders are given, activity starts, activity is monitored - that's supervision - and then an analysis is conducted of what has happened and what has not happened for the better understanding of the success or otherwise of the operation so that another time it might go better. So what he is describing is the complete process from decision to execution and then to feedback of -- at the end of an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 56 of your report, that can be found at 19 in the English and 16 in the B/C/S translation, you opine that: "The VRS communication system appears to be diverse and robust." Did you find any support for this opinion in your review of General Milovanovic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, as the Chief of Staff, concentrates very largely on the process of reporting and information flow, and talks about the issue of directives, he talks about the issuing of orders, the use of secure telephone, of radio, and he makes it quite clear that a very important part of effective functioning of the command of the army is the flow of information upwards from subordinate headquarters and subordinate formations for the better understanding and subsequent decision-making process of the superior headquarters. And as with other well-organised armies, there is always a redundancy in communication methods to ensure that if one method of communication is jammed or, say, radios are not functioning well, that information can still get through by another means, and that is a normal procedure, to make sure that a superior and subordinate headquarters can stay in touch with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn your attention to General Mladic personally as the commander of the General Staff -- of the Main Staff, I apologise. In paragraph 39 of your report, you make the following statement: "In practice, even if not according to VRS regulations, General Mladic exhibited all the characteristics of a hands-on army commander." Can I ask you to expound on that? In particular, what were those characteristics?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, it's clear to me from things I have read, television reports and video clips that I have seen, that General Mladic was a very effective commander, and that he kept close control on -- on what happened. I suppose the most obvious example, and it's a well publicised example, is to look at his activities in Srebrenica in July 1995. Srebrenica was in the area of operations of the Drina Corps but it was the focus of activity at that time, so it could be called as the army's main effort at that time, and therefore it was not unreasonable that General Mladic, as the army commander effectively, went forward into the Drina Corps area to see what was going on. And it's quite obvious from the material that I reviewed that he exercised a large measure of personal control as to what was going on. There are three meetings, for example, in the Fortuna hotel which he chaired those meetings. There is video coverage of him moving through the town, giving direction. So what this says to me is that this is very much a hands-on army commander. He was known, and I've mentioned it before this morning, to be a big character who people certainly respected and I suspect feared a certain amount as well. And therefore, what he said and what he ordered, people were likely to do. And I think in that way I'm trying to sum up what I mean when I describe him as a hands-on commander. He was not remote in some distant headquarters but he liked to be forward, exercising personal control. And that is a perfectly reasonable way of military activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you misspoke when you were talking about the "Fortuna hotel" and that you intended to refer to the "Fontana Hotel"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you're absolutely right. My apologies, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic testified that Mladic located himself in the Sarajevo area at the beginning of the war. Would this be consistent with what you have now described as a hands-on approach?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It would be consistent with the commander going to what I've -- I would describe as the point of main effort, by which I mean where the most significant activities are going on. That is where a commander would want to place himself so that he has a good feel and a good understanding of the situation in the most critical area at the time. And not surprisingly, Sarajevo being the capital of Bosnia, very much the centre of activity certainly in the early years, it doesn't surprise me at all that that's where he chose to locate himself so that he knew what was going on and could influence what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At paragraph 62 of your report, you discuss the concept of Fingerspitzengefuhl or finger-tip control. Could I ask you to describe what relationship, if any, there is between the concepts of hands-on control and the concept of Fingerspitzengefuhl?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for introducing yet another German term. But in military theory, the Germans did largely shape the lexicon. Fingerspitzengefuhl is a term understood to mean how a commander develops an instinctive sense of how things are and how things should be and how he thinks he wants things to develop. You can do that not necessarily being present on the ground. You can do it by gathering information, analysing and understanding and giving orders and direction. But often part of that sensing what is really significant takes you to the point of main effort, to the place that is the focus of activity at the time. So there is an overlap between Fingerspitzengefuhl, this sense of knowing what was going on, being able to direct sensitively what was going on, with actually being present, and the notion of being a hands-on commander is a sub-function, if you like, of the Fingerspitzengefuhl that I've been describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 60 of your report, which can be found at e-court page 20 in the original and 17 in the translation, you make the following statement: "However, whether physically present or not, a commander remains responsible for the actions of the troops under his command or in some circumstances within his delegated TAOR. Indeed, radio telephone intercepts discussed elsewhere in this statement demonstrate clearly that Mladic received reports and gave orders whether or not he was physically present at the scene of action." Can I ask you to elaborate on that and explain how you came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The point that I'm trying to make is that a commander is responsible for a plan that he develops in fulfilment of a particular mission, and in some circumstances, and this is why I use the term "TAOR," tactical area of responsibility, in some forms of conflict, and I think the Bosnian war is one of those forms of conflict, whereby the territory under dispute is divided into tactical areas of responsibility. Everything that goes on within an area of responsibility is exactly that, it is -- it remains the responsibility of the commander. So whether he or she is physically present actually is not the relevant issue. Tasks can be delegated but responsibility can never be delegated. If you've made yourself responsible for an operation and for a plan, it is your responsibility, even though you've delegated the execution of it. And within a conflict which has territorial subdivisions, then what goes on in your tactical area of responsibility remains your responsibility, and that is the point that I'm trying to make here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 80, you discuss the operational challenges of transporting all of the people in Potocari out of that location. You say: "At the outset, however, the military must bear in mind that once it sets out to move a large body of civilians from one place to another, then under international law the military takes on certain responsibilities and has certain legal obligations." My question to you is the following: Under what circumstances would it be appropriate for a military force to physically move such a large group of people?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The legitimate use of military force is against other military forces. Earlier today I've talked about the expression "war among the people," and the responsible military commander has to think about the safety of civilians and non-combatants within his tactical area of responsibility or within the geographic area of an operation that he's going to carry out. And therefore, it may be the responsible thing to do to offer to the civilian non-combatants in an area the opportunity to leave that area for their own safety. And indeed, that offer might have to include the provision of transport to remove them. I use the word "offer" because I think that is the appropriate way to go about it. Compelling people to leave their home is probably verging on the internationally legally unacceptable. And certainly compelling people to move or compelling people to move would be the wrong thing to do. The correct action to take would be to so shape your military operations that you avoid a centre of population, if that population has chosen to stay put. But in this case, it looks as if there were a large body of people that, for one reason or another, were to be moved. Whether it was voluntary or involuntary, the fact of the matter is they were going to be moved, and that elements of the VRS took responsibility for moving that large number of people from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P363 be brought to our screens. This is a portion of the military notebook of General Mladic. Could I ask that we go to e-court page 4 in both copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, I want to show you an entry from General Mladic's military notebook, and this entry records a meeting in Dobanovci, the outskirts of Belgrade on the 15th of July, 1995. Attending that meeting were Milosevic, Stoltenberg, Akashi, Bildt and Generals de la Presle and Smith. Now, we can see at the bottom of this page that Mladic records a separate meeting between himself, de la Presle and General Smith. Do you know General Smith, General Rupert Smith?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I know General Smith well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can see that General Mladic -- just be a moment now to call up the next page. We can see here that General Mladic records a statement by General Smith. I want to draw your attention to the paragraph that begins with the number 4. Mladic writes down what Smith is saying. He records: "Treatment of the population in Srebrenica and Zepa. There are rumours about atrocities, massacres and rape." My first question to you is: Based on your training and extensive experience as a commander, what would be the likely purpose of one commander telling another commander about information regarding crimes being committed by that second commander's troops?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, if one commander tells another commander that he has got information or he has heard rumours of improper or illegal activity being conducted by the other commander's troops, as would appear to be the case here in the conversation between General Smith and General Mladic, then the responsible action of the other party, the one against whom allegations were being made, would be to initiate some kind of investigation. Of course, I do not know whether this did indeed occur, but certainly if I had been a party to that conversation, and someone had made an allegation, I would feel honour-bound and obliged to investigate. And to give a more up-to-date example, when I was head of the British army, from time to time allegations were made of improper actions by British soldiers either in Iraq or Afghanistan, and one understands the absolute importance of investigating openly and transparently these rumours, these claims, to either be able to dismiss them authoritatively or if there is substance to them, then to have a more detailed investigation, and if necessary bring about perpetrators of improper or illegal acts to the judicial system and if necessary bring them before a court. And this, sadly, in the odd occasion, in the experience of the British army is something that we've had to do but it's the right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that we see another notebook entry from later in July. It is P345. And the entry I'm interested in begins in e-court page 229.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, while that's being brought to our screens, we now know that General Mladic, upon receiving this information from General Smith, did not return to Srebrenica but, instead, attended wedding of a friend the next day. In your view, was that appropriate for a commander of forces that has received information of such possible atrocities? Ignore the --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It hasn't come up on the screen, but it doesn't matter. I think it's surprising that if allegations of that substance have been made, that a commander should choose to go to a wedding, a social occasion, rather than vigorously follow up and start to investigate the circumstances. I can't get inside the head of General Mladic over that day or two, but it does seem quite surprising to me that if he took General Smith's allegations seriously, that he wasn't that concerned that he would wanted to have followed up as thoroughly as possible and not wanted to have seen to have trivialised the allegations by himself going to a social event, going to a wedding. I find it surprising that he put himself in what I would regard as an inappropriate situation and open himself up to criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may intervene, Mr. Groome. Mr. Dannatt, is it not permissible or possible that a commander in that situation could give orders to his next in chief, his right-hand man, to undertake the investigations or any other one that he thought appropriate could do the job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's entirely possible, and may well be what happened. I think the point that I'm trying to make is that if these allegations were as serious and significant as they were, I just ask the question as to whether the most senior commander, the person most responsible, was perhaps being wise to be seen at a social event at a time of great sensitivity and great difficulty. His presence at the wedding didn't stop an investigation, but the question I ask, and I haven't got the answer, is whether it was the right place for him to be, given serious events that had been alleged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have also a question. Do you consider this to be within your expertise because what is wise or not, where to show up, if you have -- let's just for argument's sake assume that orders were given for an investigation or were not given, but, apart from that, is the fact whether it's wise, isn't that more a policy matter rather than that it has got anything to do with command and control of an army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An aspect of command and control, sir, is judgement, and the wise use of judgement. I think it's perfectly proper, as a military expert, to just ask the question: Was General Mladic on that day in question correct in making the decision to go to a wedding when serious allegations had been made against his army. It's merely a matter of judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you remain seated. Mr. Mladic, you remain seated. Apparently counsel would like to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, volume. Inaudible. I think the usher has misunderstood me. "Inaudible" is an instruction for Mr. Mladic that he speak -- Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, Judges Moloto and Orie have both raised with you the possibility of Mladic, upon receiving this information from General Smith, of giving orders to undertake an investigation of such a matter. In your review of the materials that you were given to study, did you see any evidence or anything that indicated to you that upon receipt of this information, General Mladic gave an order in response to it or to initiate an investigation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I -- I don't believe that I have seen anything. But, again, I only know what I know and there may be documents that I'm not aware of or other material that I'm not aware of which would have indicated that he had initiated an investigation, but I've not seen anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I can draw your attention to the screen before you, where we now have P345 on our screens - it's e-court page 229 - we can see in this entry from General Mladic's notebook that he records a meeting on the morning of 24 July 1995, a time when information about what happened in Srebrenica is now publicly known. He's meeting with President Milosevic and General Perisic, the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav army. He records Milosevic saying, "Srebrenica and Zepa have damaged us greatly." If the president of a neighbouring and supportive country, in the presence of the commander of its army, tells the VRS commander that what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa has caused great damage, would such information be a basis for that commander to initiate an investigation into what exactly happened and who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm not sure if you have the right page in B/C/S on the screen. Could you please check that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not speaking B/C/S, I'll see what I can do, Your Honour. But perhaps Mr. Ivetic can assist us. I think it might help if we have the transcription of the notebook instead of the digital version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because you are referring to the entry at 0930 hours. This could be the lower part of it but it's nearly illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll be guided by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think apart from legibility, it looks as if we have the right page on our screen, Mr. Ivetic. Would you confirm that, the first bullet point starting with what seems to be "SM"? I think we have the right one in B/C/S at this moment, unless it's challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told it appears to be the right page, although very illegible on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may consult with my client, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least if Mr. Mladic speaks with a volume so soft that no one can hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my client was just indicating that he has difficulty reading on his monitor and would ask for a hard copy of this page, if the Prosecution has it available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it in order to follow the questions or in order to verify whether it really says what it says? Because, as you know, there is a transcripted version in B/C/S as well, if we would have that on our screen. But I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He needs to be able to do both, but primarily to follow the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- it's an extremely brief entry, perhaps if I simply read it and then we will do our best to try to find a copy that Mr. Mladic can read later on. It says: "Meeting with President Milosevic and General Perisic. SM, Srebrenica and Zepa have damaged us very greatly. You must have a political dimension in the post of the commander of the army. I wanted to prove to everyone that you are a serious man." That's the end of the entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have not read everything, Mr. Groome. The first bullet point starts with an asterisk and then SM, then we have a second bullet point without at least explicitly a speaker identified and then we have a third bullet point. So you read it but without the layout as we find it, at least in the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should add that this is an entry Belgrade 24th of July, 1995, 930 hours, as indicated in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, if I can return to my question: If a commander receives this information, would this be a sufficient basis to initiate an investigation into what exactly happened in Srebrenica and Zepa and who, if anyone, might be responsible within the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: In my view, this is a pretty serious comment made by Mr. Milosevic. I'm assuming that the three bullet points are comments that Mr. Milosevic, President Milosevic, made. And if they were being made to me and if I was General Mladic as a party to that meeting, I would actually feel rather embarrassed. The allegation that Srebrenica and Zepa -- and one has to assume that we are not talking about the military attack to capture those towns but whatever may have happened subsequently, I'd be embarrassed that actually that was damaging. I would be embarrassed that I was being told as an army commander that I must be sensitive to politics and to the political dimension of my role as an army commander. And I would be embarrassed that the president of another country is saying, Look, I really want to help and to get everyone to understand that you actually are a serious man. My take-away from all that is that if I hadn't initiated an investigation to find out what had happened and who was responsible, I would be -- my embarrassment would have turned into anger and I would have gone straight away to get to the bottom of this because being told off, if you like, by the president of another country is embarrassing. I keep using the word embarrassing. And embarrassment turns to anger pretty quickly and I would have done something about it. What was done, I'm not entirely sure. That's my -- that's my interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I move to the next document, Ms. Stewart has printed a hard copy of this entry, if I could have the assistance of the usher to provide that to the Defence who can in turn provide it to Mr. Mladic if he needs to read it. Could I ask that 65 ter 02261 be brought to our screens. That may take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But this is a document, it's an evaluation of Major-General Radislav Krstic for a period which includes July 1995. This appraisal was done on the 6th of November, 1995, well after what happened at Srebrenica was public knowledge. Before I take you to a passage in the document, can I ask you whether you are familiar with the use of staff appraisals in the military and, if so, what function do they fulfil?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I'm very familiar with the process of staff appraisals. In the British army it is usual for everyone at whatever rank to receive an annual report on their activities and conduct, and the -- there are two principle purposes of the annual appraisal: One is to help an individual improve their capability, to improve their performance; and secondly, it's to evaluate their suitability for promotion to a higher rank or to another appointment, perhaps a more demanding appointment. So I am very familiar with the process. And when I first saw this document, I was very interested, being very familiar with British army processes and procedures, to see how the Army of the Republika Srpska conducted such appraisals, and I've read the words that General Mladic wrote about General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to the second page and if we focus on a section entitled, "Description and conclusion." And if we read it we can see that Mladic writes positive and detailed comments about Krstic's service throughout the war, including during the time of Srebrenica. On this last page of his appraisal, he assesses Krstic's performance as, "Excellent." In fact, the last phrase of the appraisal states: "General Krstic is one of the most successful and most promising generals of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "... most promising generals of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your experience as a commander, if we accept that Mladic was sincere in his praise of General Krstic, does this indicate anything about Mladic's intention regarding what happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I do find this -

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question. It calls for speculation and goes beyond the expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Dannatt has explained the use of such appraisals in the military system. I'm simply asking him now what would this indicate about General Krstic's conduct in Srebrenica given the comments that we find here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the question as it's now rephrased, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If that's the question that's being asked, I would ask -- yeah, then I don't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, could I ask your assistance and perhaps read again the second question, the question as rephrased by Mr. Groome, and answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just reading that now, sir, and I'll endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, it's now the third time today that I have to ask you to keep your voice at a low volume. I'm not intending to repeat that again and again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Endeavouring to answer the question as phrased, my understanding, General Mladic, as the army commander, is writing a report on one of his corps commanders, General Krstic in this case, and in grading him excellent is approving of his conduct as a successful general. The problem that I have, and it's not for me to try and answer the question, is we know as a matter of fact that around 8.000 men and boys met an untimely death at Srebrenica and someone was responsible for that. General Krstic was the commander of the Drina Corps and these untimely deaths took place within the Drina Corps area of operations. We have to assume that this was not an activity that was ordered by General Mladic or ordered by General Krstic, so one has to assume that some illegal activity took place on a very large scale. Well, if that was the case, I can't really see how General Krstic's performance could be considered to be excellent in the way that General Mladic describes. His performance early in the war might have been, but this big question mark over how 8.000 men and boys came to meet an untimely death in the Drina Corps area stands as a very big question mark. So I'm surprised, as a professional officer, that the grading of excellent can be given when such a large question mark is out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Dannatt, my final question to you is the following: The question of whether General Mladic has committed any crimes is for the Chamber. That is beyond your remit. What is properly within your remit is whether you have an opinion as to whether General Mladic, from a purely military perspective, is responsible for the conduct of his subordinates and their actions related to the city of Sarajevo, to areas in Bosnia under the control of the VRS, and in what happened related to Srebrenica. Do you have an opinion as to that, from a purely military perspective?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. It infringes upon the purview of the Chamber and is overly broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber understands the questions have been asked and have been answered because the witness told us that responsibility cannot be delegated, and therefore that includes in the understanding of the Chamber, unless the witness would say that's not true, that you have a military responsibility for what is done by your subordinates because you can't delegate your responsibility. And this is of course a rather abstract statement, but the Chamber considers the question to have been asked and to be answered. Unless we have misunderstood your answer, Mr. Dannatt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, you've understood my previous answers correctly. Tasks can be delegated. Responsibility cannot be delegated. But where one has concerns about things that people under your command have done in carrying out tasks that have been delegated to them, remembering that you are personally responsible, then to investigate and to, if necessary, bring to court, is an important part of your discharge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, you are extending the question a bit and saying what does that entail to be responsible, but you have answered that question now to some extent as well. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can just follow up Your Honour's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Judge Orie takes your previous answer to be a response to this last question but said that it was a rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But that it was a rather abstract statement. Can I ask you to apply that abstract -- the concept to your study of documents and other evidence related to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, I think we have to come back to the documents that we were discussing a few minutes ago when it would seem that on one occasion General Smith made reference to rumours of rape, massacre and killings, and President Milosevic made reference to such things being damaging, and applying that to my earlier answer, that you can't delegate responsibility, so if you are concerned about things that have happened effectively in your name, then the only responsible thing that you can do is to begin to investigate to find out where the truth lies and if other people have done wrong things, then they, rather than you, need to be brought to account, because if you don't do that, you are making yourself liable to be negligent in not fulfilling your responsibilities to ensure good order and military discipline. So negligence and not doing the right thing is an important part of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. It's time for a break. Mr. Dannatt, we now take a break of 20 minutes. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes past mid-day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to tender 65 ter 2261, that is the evaluation of General Krstic. I would do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2261 receives number P2631, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'll start with a matter but if Mr. Dannatt comes in I might stop it. I would like to deal with the subpoena for witness RM225, which was issued on the 22nd of April of this year. To put matters short, I don't think that witness will further be called to testify and I'll deal with it later, but perhaps you'll think about what the consequences should be, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, general.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, I would like to ask if you consider yourself to be an expert on the topics of the JNA, the Yugoslav All People's Defence doctrine and the Territorial Defence or TO system which was in place in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I have made some study of those things, and I believe I'm fairly conversant with them, in the wider context of my other military studies and my 40 years as an officer in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, based upon all that do you consider yourself an expert or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider your expertise on these topics to cover the entire history and origin of the JNA, the All People's Defence doctrine, and the Territorial Defence system from their inception to their conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I have made considerable study into those things. How do you define expert? Do I -- are you asking me if I know absolutely everything? I think I would find it difficult to say yes. If you are asking me whether I have a sufficient knowledge to be able to offer comment within the wider context of the matters in hand, then my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Using your own definition of expert, do you consider yourself to be an expert on the topic of the VRS, the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I would make the same answer to you. I have made considerable study of the VRS within the wider context of the matters in hand, and I think I am able to offer an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you consider your expertise as to the VRS to cover and include the entirety of the time period of 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
