utterances.text: Without wishing to be boring and repetitious, I could not claim to know everything that had occurred between 1992 and 1995, but I have looked at a number of issues, I have been present in Bosnia at various times between 1992 and 1995, and I think I have sufficient understanding to offer the Court some opinion, and that is why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to meet with and participate in exchanges with JNA officers or former JNA officers in any of the years prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from the expert reports that you have authored for the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in the Krstic case and in this case, have you authored any articles or other publications on the command and control doctrines of the JNA, the VRS or the Yugoslav All People's Defence doctrine?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you have published a book, I believe, which you mention at paragraph 22 of your expert statement in this case. Would you agree with me that this book is more of an autobiography rather than being an authoritative text on the command doctrine of either the JNA or the VRS or the Yugoslav All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I believe on the cover of the book, it says, "the autobiography" which I think answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, in your statement, with respect to this book that you're now saying is just an autobiography, you also say it is in part a study of leadership. That is what I'm asking you. Is it an autobiography or is it also to be considered an authoritative study on leadership including command and control concepts?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It certainly has a lot of coverage on leadership and aspects of command and control. I don't think because it's described as an autobiography it disqualifies itself from being a discussion of leadership. And throughout the 12 chapters of the book, there are significant passages relating to my experience on leadership and right throughout the book, either implicitly or specifically, is reference to command and control and my own experience of it. I don't see any inconsistency there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could briefly take a look at P2629 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This would be your expert statement. And if we could turn to page 3 in both versions, and I'd like to focus on paragraph 11 of the same, and here you talk about the time you spent as an instructor and you mention that part and parcel of the syllabus of the course was the comparative study of other armies' command and control procedures. Did any of those comparative studies which you taught involve the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: To the extent that the armed forces of the SFRY have their doctrinal antecedents in the wider doctrinal basis of the Soviet Union and Warsaw Pact armies, then the answer is -- is yes. And furthermore, we made extensive study of the Warsaw Pact in the round, of which one includes the JNA at the time, and therefore by wider implication, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What years was the JNA a member of the Warsaw Pact, general?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think the point that I'm trying to make is the wider doctrinal understanding of the JNA is influenced by the Soviet style of command and the -- many members of the JNA attended staff courses and courses of instruction in Russia, and therefore the general doctrinal understanding flows from that significant influence of the Russian army and the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact down into the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As an expert are you unable to answer my question as to what years the Yugoslavs were part of the Warsaw Pact, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you also mention that you authored the revised British war fighting doctrine known as the manoeuvrist approach to operations. This is, I believe, in paragraph 22 of your statement, which is on page 5 in the English, page 5 in the Serbian. Would you agree with me that this doctrine which you and your team authored is inapplicable and irrelevant to the study of the VRS and our work here today?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I don't think I would argue that it was directly applicable. I believe that mention of it is made in my statement as an indication that I have a considerable understanding of the importance of doctrine and the importance of an army having a doctrine which conditions the way that it thinks appropriate to a given set of circumstances. And the task that I was given was writing a military doctrine appropriate for the British army in the post-Cold War years. That is the claim that I'm making and I think that claim is substantiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't take dispute with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the first page of your statement, P2629 marked for identification, and if we could focus on paragraph 4 of the same. Here, sir, you say that you have had certain documentary materials made available to you by the Office of the Prosecution and that you have reviewed the same and can comment on the same. My first question in this regard is to inquire if you maintained a log of all such documentation provided to you by the Prosecution for this review?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I didn't maintain a log as such, but there is another document which we have referred to which lists for the helping of the Court the documents that I've looked at and have ascribed to them a number relevant to this case so that they can be identified. And I don't have it in front of me at the present moment, but it runs to about three or four pages of documents, and they are all listed as to what their content is and there is a number pertinent to this case that is attributed to each of those documents. So that constitutes the list of documents that I've looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the list you're referring to is entitled, "Index to material cited in expert report of General Dannatt, 23 April 2012," and the copy I have only identifies documents that you have actually cited within your statement. Is that the same list that you are talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Could I see that document on the screen in front of me, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it uploaded already, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's marked for identification as P2630.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is this, sir, the chart that you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does this identify each and every single document that you reviewed that was provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor for the performance of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: My recollection, and I put this report together some 18 months ago, when I thought I was first going to be giving evidence in this trial, is that this list is documents that I certainly looked at, and I refer to in my report. Whether each and every one is referred to in my report, I'm afraid I couldn't confirm without actually going back through it again myself at this stage, but the intention of producing this list was so that there could be numbers pertinent to this case for the better information and assistance of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, I think that there is some misunderstanding to the extent that what Mr. Ivetic apparently wants to know is whether apart from the documents you refer to explicitly in your report, whether there are other documents which you have reviewed but which you did not explicitly refer to in your report. Now, this list seems to be the index to the material which was cited. Mr. Ivetic would like to know whether there are materials you have not cited so that he has a complete overview of the material which you reviewed and which may be at the basis of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understood that to be his question as well, and there was other material, but he had asked me earlier whether I had a log of it and I don't have a log of it, so if the next question is what else have you looked at, I can't answer that question as I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, that would have been your next question, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this corpus of documentation which was provided for you, was that something that the Office of the Prosecutor had preselected for you, or did you have a hand in telling them what kind of materials to provide?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, as was made clear earlier this morning, I have taken part in a previous trial within the ICTY and also another case involving Bosnia and Serbia and, therefore, in the course of those two trials, those two cases, and this, I've looked at quite a wide amount of material. With regard to this case in particular, there were some documents that the Office of the Prosecutor drew to my attention, but this list that's in front of you does not represent a reading list, if you like, that the Office of the Prosecutor gave to me. Many of these documents I'd seen some 12, 13, 14 years ago when I was preparing for the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just briefly go back to the preparations that you undertook in the Krstic case to prepare an expert report. At that -- at that time, was documentation preselected for you by the Office of the Prosecutor and given to you to review for purposes of doing your expertise?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I had some extensive preparation for that trial, for that case, including several lengthy meetings with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, with investigators, and indeed I spent some time on the ground in Bosnia looking at these matters. So it was a fairly wide-ranging preparation that I made before that trial, to have a good understanding of the background, the ground on which the events took place, and indeed subsequently, I was back in Bosnia a year or so after I'd given evidence and returned to that ground on several occasions. So my understanding of the issues, my understanding of the background, is rather broader than just looking at a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. We are taking one by one. I'd like to stay with the documents and I'd like to get an answer to my original question. Were you given a corpus of documents by the Office of the Prosecutor that had been preselect for you for you to do your expertise in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, there were some documents that I was given to look at. That was not the totality of my research and the totality of my preparation for the case. I think it would have been surprising were that not to be the case, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could return to your statement, P2629 marked for identification, and while we wait for that, sir, did you write this statement on your own or were there others that assisted you in its preparation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The statement in this case draws fairly extensively on the statement that I had made and prepared for the Krstic case, which I drafted -- just checking my own recollection to make sure I'm factually accurate because this was back in 1999. I recall drafting myself. In this particular case, I was assisted by someone with a legal background who assisted me draw up this particular statement, but like everything that goes under your signature or above your signature, every word in it I'm content with and every word I own. So whether it was part drafted by me and part assisted by another, I would regard as immaterial. I signed that statement and I own the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the individual with the legal background who may have assisted you in drafting parts of it, could you tell us under whose employ was that individual at the time that he assisted you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The person concerned, so we are not beating about the bush, is my daughter-in-law, Lucinda Dannatt. She is a human rights lawyer in her own standing and has worked on a number of cases in a number of courts. At the time she was not working, being the mother of three small children, and to answer technically your question, who paid her, I think I did, out of the small amount of money that the court made available to me for my time in preparation for the case. So I can't remember the vast sums involved, which were not vast, but I paid her for her time myself. Because, frankly, I'll be absolutely honest, the Krstic case was hugely time consuming. The time I was serving in the army and I regarded it as part of my duty -- I still regard it as part of my duty, but having retired from the army and doing many other things the amount of time I needed to prepare properly for this case was more than I could actually make available myself, and therefore I invited my daughter-in-law, who has, as I say, some experience of working in these sorts of cases, to assist me, and I'm very grateful for her support.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could just finish up with this topic I'd like to call up 1D1448 in e-court and while we wait for that, sir, I can let you know that this ought to be a copy of some extracts from your book, if I've gotten the number right. I apparently have. If we can turn to page 11 of the version in e-court. It should correlate to pages 218 and 219 of the underlying book. At the top of the left-hand column, you have, I believe, here a reference to -- I'll just read it. It says: "As it turned out, later on my eldest son Tom's wife, Lucinda, was to work as an international criminal lawyer for the International Criminal Court in The Hague, and then in Sarajevo, work I followed with great interest and approval." Sir, could you clarify for us whether, in fact, your daughter-in-law, who is referenced here and who assisted you with the report, worked for the International Criminal Court or for this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Now you're asking a very narrow question. It's a very good question. And if I'm pursuing truth, I've got to say I'm not sure. I know she lived and worked in Sarajevo for quite a while and has done work here in The Hague. If my description in that paragraph is loose, then loose it is, but I think -- I would like to think that you and the Chamber would understand that I'm trying to explain probably to a lay audience that this is her line of work and that was some of her experiences. If it's a narrow point you want to make, you've probably made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To me, it's more important just to know what branch she worked for. Was it the Prosecution, the Defence or some other entity, if you know? If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: To be honest, I'd be speculating. I can't remember. She's moved on to a number of other cases of fairly exotic nature most recently on the Defence side. In fact, the one she is currently involved with is a fairly high profile international case, and, again, she is on the Defence side. So she is not a prosecutor per se, she will follow the work, as lawyers often do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I'd like to return to your witness statement, P2629 marked for identification, and I'd like to return to the first page where we were before this little digression. At paragraph 4, you identify that the principal documents on which you have focused appear to be reports authored by another proposed expert of the Prosecution, Richard Butler. Is that an accurate reading of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly Richard Butler's work, I studied extensively and I found it very informative, and accepted his status as someone who understood much of the circumstances of the matters in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mr. Butler'S rank and position in the US armed forces was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Short answer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was it that led you to identify Mr. Butler's work as being authoritative on the topics that are identified? Was his work known to you prior to being contacted to be an expert for the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No, I first came across Mr. Butler in preparation for the Krstic case and read the material that he had provided. And I'm just going back into my own recollection and I believe I met him and talked with him in the preparation of the Krstic case, but I could be mistaken there. But my recollection is that I have met him and was impressed by him and certainly informed and interested by his opinions and the written material that he'd produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to his report, sir, are those written materials which would have been preselected and provided for you by the Office of the Prosecutor or did you come across them by some other means?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No. I came across them because having been invited -- I think the background, as I recall it, was that the Chamber, I think the senior prosecutor - I'm just grasping for what would be the right answer here - approached the British army in 1999 to ask for a senior general to act as an expert witness for the enlightenment of the Court on matters relating to command and control - and you see them listed in paragraph 3 - and the Chief of the General Staff of the day, knowing of my own background, asked whether I was prepared to be that expert witness. At which I said yes. And at that point, came to The Hague. I met senior Prosecutor, I met the Prosecution team, and our conversations went on from there. So I don't claim to have had any great prior knowledge of General Krstic and the Krstic case before being invited to help the Court in its understanding of military command and control and took a detailed interest in the Krstic case. So perhaps not surprisingly, much of the material initially that was made available to me was made available to me by the Office of the Prosecutor because they, for the enlightenment of the Court, are the ones who had engaged me to get involved, to study, to write a report, which I've already said was very time consuming, spend time on the ground in Bosnia looking at the issues around Srebrenica, and then coming to The Hague to give my evidence. So I didn't do this because I thought it was a good idea, I did it because my commanding general invited me to do it at the invitation of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you perform any research into the professional background and prior publications of Mr. Butler to assure yourself of the experience, expertise and reliability of Mr. Butler's work on the topics of these reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think I took Mr. Butler's work and credentials at face value, and certainly having read his reports, this seemed to be a reasonable supposition to make, that he was someone of integrity and someone of ability and that, therefore, the product of his research and his writings was something one could place a sufficient degree of credibility on to make use of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you only review Mr. Butler's various reports or were you given access to Mr. Butler's testimony in other cases before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: May I just clarify your question? Is that a question relating to my preparation for the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In total, the Krstic case and this case. If there is differences, if you could please identify wherein lies the difference.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The answer to both questions in that case or both parts of the question is that I have not looked at Mr. Butler's testimony in other cases beyond the Krstic case and the extent to which there was material relating to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I then understand your testimony to mean that you have reviewed the transcript or the recording of Mr. Butler's testimony in this case, the Mladic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Again, let me just clarify the question. Are you asking if I have read Mr. Butler's -- the transcript of Mr. Butler's testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: The answer is no, I have not. And to be honest, I haven't got time to do that. I am quite a busy person and I've prepared myself in the best way that I can to give my evidence. And, actually, I don't think I really would want to have spent time reading many other people's points of view. General Milovanovic is a very interesting separate case in point because of his unique position as the deputy to General Mladic, and I've been fascinated, as I said earlier, to have read his transcript and I'm very grateful to the Office of the Prosecutor for having made it available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, the reason I ask is because Mr. Butler has testified in this case and that in order to understand his reports and understand corrections that he has made to his reports, one would have needed to review prior transcripts of his testimony. Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can -- first of all, at the time when you were first approached to prepare an expertise for the Krstic case, did you or anyone on your behalf undertake to perform a review or survey of all the literature that was out there on these topics?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: If you're suggesting a comprehensive survey of the material that was out there, no. I think I've already said, and I'm perfectly content to say, that my start point was my initial visit here to meet the staff of the Office of the Prosecutor who made certain material available to me, which gave me a way into the case. And from that, I was able to expand my own inquiries, and, indeed, as I've said, had extensive discussions with investigators and also spend time on the ground in relation to the Srebrenica aspects of the Krstic case. So my way in was undoubtedly through material provided to me by the Office of the Prosecutor and I have no difficulty personally with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to the very last page in both versions of your statement, paragraph 110 relates to an opinion or I should say an assessment about the quality of Mr. Butler's various reports, and I want to ask you why is this in here? Was this something that either the Office of the Prosecutor or Mr. Butler asked you to include as part of your expertise in this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Can I just clarify that you're talking about paragraph 110 and not paragraph 109?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that 109 and 110 refer to the exact same reports. Please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I think, well, you're right. It's just that 109 is rather more definitive in that actually it references Richard Butler's work. Now, I'm going to be honest, absolutely, with you. I can't remember. I produced this report 18 months ago, and, inevitably, there were some iterations of that report. And truthful answer to your question is whether this was something I wanted to put in or whether in discussion it therefore seemed sensible to put in, but the fact of the matter is paragraphs 109 and 110 are above my signature, and they are my words and my opinion and they stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the question remains -- yes, Mr. Dannatt, sorry, the question remains. Whether you take responsibility for what is said there doesn't answer the question who took the initiative to adopt those two paragraphs or at least paragraph 110 in the report. I mean, these are two entirely different questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the avoidance of any doubt at all, all the words in the 110 paragraphs of my statement are words that I own and I take responsibility for. They are my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it still doesn't answer the question about even if you accept full responsibility for the text, that doesn't answer the question who thought about adopting this text and make it part of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I just stand by what I said a little while ago. I put this together 18 months ago and I genuinely can't remember, and I think that's the honest and fair answer to your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and the answer would be guessing and I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you characterise the type of study that you did of the VRS as including an extensive study of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, again, we are into semantics now and what is extensive and what is not extensive. But what I found absolutely fascinating was -- this is the relevant bit, as far as I'm concerned, is to look into the origins of the Army of Republika Srpska which clearly came from a military district of the JNA, and that is -- I think we would all agree that that is the factual course of what happened, and it answers the question which otherwise was very much in my mind, sort of 13, 14 years ago, when I first started looking at these things. How could an army that was created in the middle of an emergency in 1992 take on command and control, take on regulations, take on substance so that it could function as an operating army, just conjured up out of nothing. And when my research showed me quite clearly that the answer to the question is the VRS took on the regulations, form and substance of a part of the JNA, that answered the question. Otherwise, creating an army out of nothing in a hurry in the middle of a civil war would have been an impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to take a look at 1D1450 with you. While we wait for it on the screen I can introduce it to you as the testimony that you gave before the International Court of Justice on 20 March 2006. If we could turn to page 3 of the same in e-court, and that will correlate to page 11 of the underlying compte rendu of the ICJ, and I would like to draw your attention to the last question and the first part of your answer. And it reads as follows: "Ms. Korner: Thank you very much, General Dannatt. I'm now going to move straight away to one of the aspects that we would like you to assist the Court with, and that is the theory of command doctrines and decision-making. Could you assist the Court with the main theory or theorys of those doctrines? "General Dannatt: Put succinctly, armies conduct their business in one of two ways. Both are characterised by a somewhat complicated German word. One is known as the Befehlstaktik approach to command and control, and the other is the Auftragstaktik method of command and control." And I'd like to stop right there and ask you in relation to this part of the answer so far, do you stand by the same as being truthful and accurate in its content such that you would repeat the same today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think the witness has explained to us that is -- was his answer today to many questions as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I think all I would say additionally, if I may, and I'll read it again, is that the transcript is not entirely accurate because it refers to commander control as opposed to command and control. So this sentence is a little bit corrupted, but I would agree with the Judge's comment. I have talked about Befehlstaktik and Auftragstaktik today. I cannot think of any reason why I should take a different view two hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, here is my question, sir, and it's very clear in the ICJ testimony, you state that there are only two ways that an army conducts its business. Is it your testimony that apart from these two German-sounding tactics, that there are -- that there is not a spectrum between the two of various command and control doctrines as understood by persons in your field?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Of course the answer is yes. When you're trying to -- as in this case I am, and in the previous case I was, trying to illuminate issues for the benefit of the Court, it's helpful, if you like, to describe a course of action and another course of action. And I think most commentators would realise that nothing in life comfortably fits into a template and that there will always be shades of grey or toning, tuning, between one side of an argument or the other side of an argument, one side of a doctrine or the other side of a doctrine. But I think it's perfectly reasonable for the illumination of a discussion to try and explain in theory one approach and to explain in theory another approach. And this is why I think military matters can often be complicated. And it's a debate that's run for a long time. Is command an art or is command a science? Actually, we would say it's an art and not a science. The use of military force may well rely heavily on technology and science but command is an intuitive thing, it's a thing in which judgement is terribly important, and we often refer to operational art as a descriptor of what a general does and in the planning of a campaign. So Befehlstaktik and Auftragstaktik describe, if you like, two sides of an argument. This is not a scientific issue. It's an artistic issue. And what I do and what you do and what General Mladic might do on a different day will be very different, but it will be informed by the overarching doctrine within which one has been brought up, and that's the point that I'm trying to make. Because just the last thing, and I've read elsewhere in some of the transcripts and some of the material, discussion about what is doctrine and what is a directive. Really important point to understand is that a doctrine, the doctrine of an army, is the way an army thinks. And the way an army thinks will heavily influence its education of its officers and its training of its officers and soldiers. Doctrine is about thought. A directive is, as the word rather implies, it is a document that directs activity. So doctrine is a thought. Directives are of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can turn to the next page of the testimony from the ICJ, I would like to discuss with you in greater detail the testimony that starts at approximately the middle of the page. And the question there is as follows: "Ms. Korner: We are going to look at a little detail about how the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army, worked and its subsequent entities. But you do respect the JNA followed the Befehlstaktik method. How are you able to say that, first of all? "General Dannatt: I can say that with a fair degree of confidence, from the result of my extensive studies, and also by way of personal example. I mentioned earlier that I was one of the commanders in Bosnia in 1995. At the particular time when we were planning the transfer from UNPROFOR to UNFOR I needed, amongst other people, to talk to General Tadic, who was then commanding one of the Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. I was not in the course of my normal duties able to get -- go to Banja Luka but I passed a message to him that I wished to meet him and indeed got to Banja Luka where I was told that he was not able to meet me as he had not received authority from General Mladic, his superior. It was quite surprising that he was not prepared to meet, because what I had to say to him would have been quite helpful in terms of the conduct of future operations. But as he had not received that clearance, he did not have the authority to meet me on his own authority and I use that as an example of a centralised type of command." Now, sir, the question I have for you is: The question very specifically directed you to focus, first and foremost, on the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and your answer talks about an incident in 1995. Am I correct that by 1995, the JNA was no longer in existence?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I find this a very interesting line of questioning which I think you're now picking out Ms. Korner for her line of questioning. I can't recall the detail of our conversation at that stage when she said, But you do respect the JNA following the Befehlstaktik model, and then I gave that example. I would probably previously have made the point that the VRS came out of the JNA and that, therefore, the same operational doctrine, Befehlstaktik model, is the one that characterised both. So I don't think it's unreasonable that I use an example of what happened in 1995. If you want to discuss that particular example, I'm very happy to do that, but I think I've failed to follow the point that you're trying to make with regard to Ms. Korner's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the record, in the document we see in front of us, there is a reference to again General Tadic. You explained earlier this morning, Mr. Dannatt, that you wanted to meet with Mr. Talic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sir. I mean this comment is shot through with mistakes. UNPROFOR to IFOR, for example, not General Tadic but General Talic and he was commanding 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka. This is full of mistakes but I don't take responsibility for that. I didn't write this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the point of my question is: As an expert preparing this very serious expertise, do you consider it to be an appropriate methodology to draw conclusions from one isolated experience, such as this incident with General Talic that indeed is recited in somewhat the same detail in paragraph 32 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think it would be an appalling way to reach a judgement. I completely agree with you. And of course that is not what I'm trying to do. But life can be quite boring at times, and to put an illustration in makes it a little more interesting and a little bit illuminating. As you know full well, I suspect, that the examples of centralised command and control which we've seen in the VRS and formerly in the JNA are frequent in the other documentation that we've listed and that we've looked at. And, of course, if you've got time, I'm very happy to talk further about that. This is an example which I thought added a little colour to the factual and theoretical material otherwise we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider that maybe General Talic didn't want to meet with you for some personal reasons of his own and just used the excuse that he had not been authorised? Is that not a plausible explanation of this as well?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: It's perfectly possible. But as I said earlier on today, the two liaison officers - and I've said earlier Captain Popovic was one and the colonel was another - were I felt a little embarrassed when they said that General Talic was unable to meet me because he had not had approval to do that and he could only have got approval from one person, and that was from General Mladic. I actually can't think of any reason otherwise why he wouldn't have wanted to meet me because I'd made it quite clear that I was trying to get to Banja Luka at some difficulty to myself to try and give him some information which probably would have been helpful in the wider -- in the wider delivery and implementation of the Dayton agreement. And I can't think of any reason why he wouldn't otherwise have wanted to meet me. It was a perfectly reasonable thing to do. Generals meet each other fairly regularly and I'd asked to see him, and had I thought he wouldn't have seen me, I wouldn't have set out on what was actually quite an awkward journey to Banja Luka to try and meet him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. Yes. Mr. Dannatt, perhaps good for you to know that advocacy is often described as an art, but Mr. Ivetic now knows that command is described as an art as well. Perhaps something to think over for the next 20 minutes. We take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to further consult, you can do it during the break, Mr. Mladic. We take a break and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, Mr. Mladic, I asked you to several times this morning not to speak aloud. When we left the courtroom it was even louder than before. Please take care that -- don't bring us in a position that we have to take measures. So if you would please do that, then we can -- you can attend the proceedings. Then the other matter I'll finish now, Mr. Groome, the Chamber takes the opportunity to state on the record, I introduced it before, that the Prosecution will not adduce the evidence of Witness RM225 and for that reason, the Chamber withdraws the subpoena and relevant parts of the corresponding request to the state where the witness resides and instructs the Registry to inform the proposed witness and the appropriate state authorities of this oral decision, and notify the Chamber when it has done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to that course of action, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've taken this action by now so therefore -- and this concludes, of course, then the decision of the Chamber on this matter. Could the witness be escorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, can I just bring to the attention of the Chamber two possible scheduling problems ahead of us. One is that this Thursday the arrangements have been made for a Polish interpreters, since the witness will be testifying in Polish. So it does require some -- if it goes beyond that we -- there will be a bit of a problem. And then earlier today Mr. Lukic informed us that he was revising his estimate for the examination of Mr. Brown up to eight hours, which, again, looking at next week, makes it a very full week and I would want to inform the Chamber that Mr. Treanor would be unavailable to carry over to the week after that. So perhaps everyone could think about that. We could take five minutes to discuss scheduling before the week is out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before the end of this week, you would say, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I propose to return to your written statement, P2629 marked for identification, page 4 in the English and page 3 in the Serbian, and paragraph 12 of the same, but at least the last sentence of paragraph 12, which is indeed on page 4 of the English. Here, you cite to meetings that you had with the senior commanders of all three warring factions. Did you ever have occasion to meet with any members of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to remember, General Gvero came to Mrkonjic Grad. If I did my research I could give you the exact date. It was the date that we were required under the terms of the Dayton agreement to return Mrkonjic Grad and an area of country around there from Croat control back to Serb control. General Gvero came on that occasion. Most of my other dealings were not with Main Staff officers but with General Talic and others in Banja Luka. And then subsequently, General Simic, I got to know well, but that was later when I was back as the NATO deputy commander in 1999 -- wrong, 2000/2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, just to stay with the meeting that you would have had with General Gvero, would that have been approximately at D- plus 90 of the --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I guess that probably was. I'm just trying to remember now the sequence of events, but that seems about right. There was a 45-day period during which the Croat forces had to leave. I think they left at D-plus 45 and at D-plus 90 VRS forces were allowed to return and I'm pretty certain that was on the day that the VRS forces came back. I could be wrong but I think that's about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, we have been using "D-plus" as a shortcut. Could we fill everyone else in on what that means?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. D was the day that the Dayton peace agreement became operative which I think was the 20th of December, 1995, or might have been the 21st, and therefore all the steps of implementation were related to that date and were known as D-plus something or rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now with respect to the meetings that you did have with General Gvero at that time and the meetings that you would have had later with General Simic, I think you mentioned, did any of those meetings serve as a basis for any of the opinions that are contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think all those sort of meetings add to your general sum of knowledge. Perhaps I could also say, and I will try and be brief, I mentioned earlier that I had been the colonel running the high commander staff course at the British army staff college, and amongst other things was therefore responsible for campaign planning and the teaching of campaign planning. I was particularly interested during the course of 1995 to see how the course of the war on the ground in Bosnia changed. From 1992 to early 1995, by and large, territory held by one side or another didn't really change hands. But in spring and early summer 1995, a major operation in the south and west of Bosnia swept the Croat and Muslim forces up through into the Krajina and then sort of hooked across, began to threaten Banja Luka. And it was interesting to me to see how fairly complex campaign had been put together. To be short about it, I then decided while I was in country, between October 1995 and April 1996, as a kind of side line to other things that I was doing, to conduct a bit of a study into how this campaign came about and came to be constructed, and I set out with one of my staff officers to interview all the commanders on the three sides, to ask them what had happened in the year before. And I discussed it with General Dudakovic, General Glasnovic of the Croatian side, and, again, General Talic was reluctant to talk to me, but the two liaison officers that I met again came to my headquarters in Sipovo and one evening they became very frank about the way that they had conducted their part of the operation. And as a result of that, I was able to put together the three accounts and come up with what was to me a fairly interesting explanation as to how these military operations had been developed. And if I appear to be digressing, I apologise, but it's indicative of a growing picture of understanding of how the war was conducted, how the various armies conducted themselves, remembering that the three competent armies were all commanded by professional officers who pretty much without exception had had their origins in the JNA. And one of the things that I recall most clearly was a commanders' conference which we had in late December, I think it was, in 1995, which was the first time we had brought senior commanders of the three armies together. And after their initial suspicion of each other, they greeted each other like the old comrades that they were, because in the main they had been at the staff college together, and it was very interesting to see that reunion across the divide. Again, I apologise if I appear to digress, but I do so to show that one had quite an interest and developed that interest professionally into how the three armies had had their origins and drew my own conclusions about that. I'm sorry if I've digressed too far, indulging myself, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do not mind it's not digression but rather speed of speech which is of concern to me at this moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my enthusiasm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two go hand in hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My enthusiasm overtaking. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to take a look at something else that you've highlighted in paragraph 6 of your statement that you have reviewed and that those are memoirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 1D1450 in e-court. And once that comes up, I would be asking for page 7 of the same to be displayed. And that should correlate to page 15 of the ICJ document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus just above the middle of the page, I think you'll see there that Ms. Korner has asked you about the number of memoirs that you have read, and your answer is as follows: "General Dannatt: Indeed it is so. People such as General Sir Michael Rose, General Sir Rupert Smith, Mr. Richard Holbrooke, all have committed their near contemporaneous records into book form. I certainly have all those books and others. One finds that the colour in those books amplifies the facts that I have picked up from the trial documents that I've studied." Does this testimony from the ICJ case accurately identify the memoirs that you reference in paragraph 6 of your statement in this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, and time has moved on and I've read other accounts. I think we all, who have had some involvement in the events in the Balkans in the 1990s, have continued to take quite a professional interest, and therefore a number of books and memoirs that I read. And, yes, I sweep all that comment into paragraph 6 when I say I have read a large number of memoirs written about the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your position that these memoirs are corroborative or supportive of your conclusions as to the JNA, the VRS, as contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I think they are corroborative. I think as I said in the ICJ transcript, what is the expression that I use here? One finds that the colour in those books amplifies the facts that I picked up from the trial documents that I've studied. I think everything -- everything sits in a context and documents are quite dry, documents are quite narrow, but when you've got a broad understanding of the context and the background into which they sit, then they make rather more sense. I think that is the point that I'm trying to make, and I think it's a -- it's a fair point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you remind us if the late Mr. Holbrooke, if he held any military rank or had any military experience?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I can't remember. I suspect someone of his generation probably had some -- I will slow down -- probably had some military experience going back to the Vietnam era, but I don't recall. But I don't think you would disagree with me that he had a very interesting insight on developments, the conclusion of the war in Bosnia and was a significant factor in driving towards what became the Dayton peace agreement. So I think his opinions and his views are of relevance and certainly of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, may I invite you to stick to the question? I mean, the question was not whether it would be interesting to read Mr. Holbrooke's book. The question simply was whether he held any military rank or had any military experience. The first four words would have done. You can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to review the books or memoirs of any former JNA officers for purposes of the study of the command doctrine and structure of the JNA or the VRS or the All People's Defence that you undertook for this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: In the interests of brevity, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of any books written by General Branko Mamula, Dr. Momcilo Lazovic or Dr. Milenko Stezevic [phoen] on the topic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Well, pursuant to my last answer, the answer again is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In terms of the documentation that was made available to you by the Prosecution for review and upon which you have relied for your opinions, did those documents include the strategy of All People's Defence and Self-Protection of the SFRY which is 65 ter number 17295 in this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't know whether something is going to come up on the screen but I'm certainly conversant with that, and in the break I was reflecting on -- I will be brief -- on part of our last conversation. When we talked about military doctrine, and I talked about doctrine being a way an army thinks, I think the concept of All People's Defence, total National Defence, is what I would describe as a strategy rather than a doctrine. It was what was formulated in the early 1940s and was the strategy that drove the JNA through to its dissolution in the early 1990s. There we are. It's on the screen in front of me. It calls itself a strategy which is why I make the distinction between a strategy and a doctrine. The language is quite loose at times when people describe military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can call up 65 ter number 17293, and that would be the 1983 JNA textbook on command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you again: Would this have been something that you had access to and reviewed for purposes of your expertise in this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: May I wait till it comes on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go maybe to the second page in English, we will see the substantive text. Do you recall dealing with this book, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I don't think I recall seeing this book, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 25695.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for it I can introduce it as the 1985 rules of service of the armed services. And again I'll ask you was this a publication that you recall having had been made available to you and upon which you relied for your work in this case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I'll be absolutely honest, I can't remember, but I looked at a number of documents going back into -- well, during the course of existence of the JNA because of their relevance to working out the origins of the Bosnian Serb Army. So whether I did or whether I didn't, I can't remember, and it may be that you're going to offer me two or three other documents. I can't recall. But I formed a good understanding of the origin of the VRS as being based in the JNA and its various regulations and documentary origins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can assist Mr. Ivetic. He's inquiring about documents that General Dannatt had access to but did not cite in the report. If I can draw his attention to an e-mail sent by the Prosecution on the 5th of July, 2012, we provided a list of all of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That will short circuit at least a few questions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and we can move on, and I thank Mr. Groome for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did have you occasion to perform any research or review into the military education regime that was in existence in the SFRY prior to 1992 for its military officers?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I didn't make a particular study into that. No, I did not make a particular study into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in the direct examination that officers were sent for training to the Soviet Union. Did you happen to know as part of your expertise and as part of your research that, in fact, Yugoslav officers were also sent for training to the United States of America; for instance, General Kadijevic, who was the Yugoslav minister of defence in 1991 and 1992, completed courses at the US army command and General Staff college while a colonel?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: That doesn't surprise me, and it relates to an earlier part of this morning's conversation, whereas we all know that the former Yugoslavia had a rather -- no, not rather, had a unique position in that it was not totally in the Warsaw Pact and of the Soviet bloc but its origins were of Soviet-type thinking, but it had developed itself into probably the most open of the communist countries. And we all found it very interesting as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you're not surprised that Mr. Kadijevic may have been trained in the US but you apparently do not know it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know that for sure. But it doesn't -- as I said, it does not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now could you tell us if you say officers were sent for training to the Soviet Union, was that in larger numbers or was that one or two or three, or were they sent by the hundreds or? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I please have a reference to where that was said this morning? I'm having trouble finding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe he mentioned sending to Moscow rather than the Soviet Union. I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, he said to Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To Russia, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps that helps to find the respective portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I suspected -- I thank Your Honour for having the attention to detail that I sometimes lack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer your specific question, sir, I don't know the numbers. But I'm aware that a number of people did go and study in Russian academies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking it because the question more or less suggests they were not only sent to Russia but also to the US, or at least they were trained there. And, therefore, my question, Mr. Ivetic, as you may understand is what was the proportion? Was it a regular thing to send them either west or east? That's something that came to my mind, and if either of the parties would have any information about it, then of course it would assist me and perhaps my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm allowed to offer a view, the preponderance of people going to foreign academies would have gone east rather than west. Because the command and control style of the JNA and the VRS was based on the centralised command and control which is the one that characterised Warsaw Pact and eastern armies. If a large number had gone to the United States military academy, one would have seen the JNA over time or the VRS moving towards espousing the western approach of Auftragstaktik, the indirect approach which I've discussed earlier. But the overriding doctrine, military thought, is the one of centralised command and control which is characterised by eastern armies and the former Soviet Union and the former Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could move to another topic also returning to your statement P2629 marked for identification, page 2 in English and page 1 through 2 in the Serbian, paragraph 5. And while we wait for that, sir, I can introduce it by saying this is in relation to the site visits that you undertook of locations in Bosnia where you were accompanied by Investigator Ruez and Prosecutor Cayley of the Prosecution. And I'd like to ask you when visiting these sites, did either Ruez or Cayley provide details to you about what they believed had happened at these locations?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Short answer to that is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you rely upon Cayley and Ruez's representations as being authoritative as to what had happened at these locations?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: In the main, I would say yes as well, but having gone to those locations, one used one's own judgement based on one's own observations of the buildings, of the burial sites, of the reburial sites, and I think it was perfectly reasonable to reach conclusions about what may or may not have happened there. But, yes, in the main, the information given to me, particularly by Jean-Rene Ruez, the French investigator, who had spent a lot of time and had gone into some great detail very much formed my opinions, I think not surprisingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider whether the information given to you by Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez was biased or unbiased before allowing it to very much form your opinions?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I don't think I would regard it as biased. The facts, as they seemed to reveal themselves, rather pointed to a certain set of conclusions. After all, we had upwards of 8.000 Muslim men and boys who had been killed, who had been buried, in many cases exhumed and reburied, in an area that was controlled by the Bosnian Serb population. So I think I was probably invited and capable of drawing my own deductions as to who may or may not have been responsible in general terms. Who was specifically responsible is, of course, not for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to 1D1448 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this will again be excerpts from your autobiography that we've previously dealt with. While we wait for that, sir, perhaps I can ask you some general questions. First of all, is this book -- does this book contain only your own words or was it ghost written or assisted to you, written by someone else either in whole or in part?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Contrary to popular expectation and common practice, I wrote that book completely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if we can turn to page 16 in the part in e-court, that will correlate to pages 258 through 259 in the -- at least the Corgi paperback edition of your book. And I'd like to go through with you what begins on the last paragraph of the left column and finishes up on the right column. And it touches upon a topic that you've already touched upon, how it was that you came to be retained as an expert, and then it gives some further details I would like to ask you questions about. So please follow along with me: "General Sir Richard Wheeler, Chief of the General Staff, rang me to ask whether I would be prepared to go to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in The Hague to give evidence as an expert witness in a trial relating to the Srebrenica massacre in 1995. I said that of course I would do this and soon found myself making a series of visits to both Bosnia and the Netherlands to prepare my evidence. The accused was General Radovan Krstic, who in July 1995 had been commanding the Drina Corps of the Bosnian Serb Army. It was alleged that his troops had carried out the massacre of nearly 8.000 Muslim men and boys around Srebrenica in the middle of July 1995. It was quite clear from the material I reviewed that the intent behind the massacre had come from the top and that Krstic's direct orders had been received from General Ratko Mladic himself. The issue before the Court was the extent of Krstic's personal involvement. To prepare for the case, I not only had extensive discussions with the Prosecution team in The Hague but visited most of the execution and burial sites with the remarkable French gendarmerie officer, Jean-Rene Ruez. He had spent years investigating the massacre and was very close to all the issues." First of all, sir, does this accurately reflect how it came to pass that you were contacted to be an expert witness for the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: Yes, that's pretty much what I said earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And one part you did not mention earlier today was that the reviewed material that convinced you that the intent behind the massacre was direct orders from General Mladic, was this a predetermination that you had arrived at before being retained as an expert for purposes of the trial in the Mladic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: I'm just reflecting on the question. And I would just look again at the words that I've got there. That was my personal opinion, and I think the transcript of my evidence in the Krstic case does not include me voicing my own opinion, but I'm entitled to reach an opinion, even if I choose not to express it. I expressed it in a book, but then a book is a book, it is not a submission to a Court and it's not delivered on oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please identify for us what were these direct orders that you say Krstic received from Mladic for a massacre? Are they written down somewhere?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT
utterances.text: No. I don't think they are written down. And I think I'm giving -- I think I'm now discussing my own opinion, an opinion expressed in a book and not an opinion expressed in court, and I think I'm entitled to my own view. You or General Mladic can take a contrary view to my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dannatt, may I -- you are engaging in a debate rather than that you're answering questions. If it is your view that your personal opinions, even if expressed publicly, are irrelevant for cross-examination, then I'm afraid that you're wrong. Mr. Ivetic is fully entitled to enquire into personal opinions, which could or could not have had an influence on your work. That's for Mr. Ivetic to decide whether he wants to explore that, yes or no, and you're invited to answer the questions as they are put to you rather than to enter into a debate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I didn't want to stop you exactly at 2.15 because I thought it was an important matter for you. That's the reason why we adjourn a couple of minutes later. Mr. Dannatt, may I invite you to stay with us for another half a minute? Mr. Ivetic, may I assume that in view of the fact that you've spent close to one and a half hour that you'll need the other, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Four hours total so that would be another two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours. Yes. So that we will conclude well in time tomorrow so as to give Mr. Groome an opportunity for re-examination, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Dannatt, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. And we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 12th of November, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of November, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.20 p.m.,
